source_text: Ἀλλ’, ὡς ἔοικεν, οἱ φιλόσοφοι τῶν Ἑλλήνων θεὸν ὀνομάζοντες οὐ γιγνώσκουσιν, ἐπεὶ μὴ σέβουσι κατὰ θεὸν τὸν θεόν. τὰ φιλοσοφούμενα δὲ παρ’ αὐτοῖς κατὰ τὸν Ἐμπεδοκλέα ὡς διὰ πολλῶν δὴ γλώσσης ἐλθόντα ματαίως ἐκκέχυται στομάτων, ὀλίγον τοῦ παντὸς ἰδόντων. ὡς γάρ που τὸ ἀπὸ τοῦ ἡλίου φῶς δἰ ὑελοῦ σκεύους πλήρους ὕδατος μεθοδεύει ἡ τέχνη εἰς πῦρ, οὕτω καὶ ἡ φιλοσοφία ἐκ τῆς θείας γραφῆς τὸ ἐμπύρευμα λαβοῦσα ἐν ὀλίγοις φαντάζεται. ναὶ μὴν ὡς τὸν αὐτὸν ἀέρα ἀναπνεῖ τὰ ζῷα ἅπαντα, ἄλλα δὲ ἄλλως καὶ εἴς τι διάφορον, οὕτως δὲ καὶ τὴν ἀλήθειαν μετίασιν οἱ πλείους, μᾶλλον δὲ τὸν περὶ ἀληθείας λόγον. οὐ γὰρ περὶ θεοῦ τι λέγουσιν, ἀλλὰ τὰ ἑαυτῶν πάθη ἐπὶ θεὸν ἀνάγοντες ἐξηγοῦνται. γέγονεν γὰρ αὐτοῖς ὁ βίος τὸ πιθανὸν ζητοῦσιν, οὐ τὸ ἀληθές· ἐκ μιμήσεως δὲ ἀλήθεια οὐ διδάσκεται, ἀλλ’ ἐκ μαθήσεως. οὐ γὰρ ἵνα δόξωμεν εἶναι χρηστοί, εἰς Χριστὸν πιστεύομεν, καθάπερ οὐδὲ εἰς τὸν ἥλιον ἕνεκά γε τοῦ φαίνεσθαι μόνον ἐν ἡλίῳ ὄντας παρερχόμεθα, ἀλλ’ ἐνταῦθα μὲν τοῦ ἀλεαίνεσθαι χάριν, ἐκεῖ δὲ τοῦ εἶναι καλοὶ καὶ ἀγαθοὶ ἕνεκα Χριστιανοὶ εἶναι βιαζόμεθα, ὅτι μάλιστα βιαστῶν ἐστιν ἡ βασιλεία, ἐκ ζητήσεως καὶ μαθήσεως καὶ συνασκήσεως τελείας τὸ γενέσθαι βασιλέα καρπουμένων. ὁ μιμούμενος ἄρα τὴν δόκησιν δολοῖ καὶ τὴν πρόληψιν. ὅταν δέ τις ἔναυσμα λαβών του πράγματος ἐξάψῃ τοῦτο ἔνδον ἐν τῇ ψυχῇ πόθῳ καὶ μαθήσει, πάντα ἐπὶ τούτοις κινεῖ πρὸς τὸ ἐπιγνῶναι. οὗ γάρ τις μὴ ἀντιλαμβάνεται, οὐδὲ ποθεῖ αὐτὸ οὐδὲ ἀσπάζεται τὴν ἐξ αὐτοῦ ὠφέλειαν. τὸ ὕστερον οὖν ὁ γνωστικὸς ἐπὶ τέλει τῶν κατορθωμάτων μιμεῖται τὸν κύριον, εἰς ὅσον ἐφικτὸν ἀνθρώποις, ποιότητά τινα κυριακὴν λαβὼν εἰς ἐξομοίωσιν θεοῦ. οἱ δὲ μὴ ἐπιστάμενοι τὴν γνῶσιν οὐδὲ κανονίζειν δύνανται τὴν ἀλήθειαν. μεταλαμβάνειν οὖν τῶν γνωστικῶν θεωρημάτων οὐχ οἷόν τε, ἐὰν μὴ τῶν προτέρων διανοημάτων κενώσωμεν ἑαυτούς. ἁπλῶς γὰρ οὕτως ἀλήθεια κοινῶς λέγεται παντὸς νοητοῦ τε καὶ αἰσθητοῦ. αὐτίκα ἔνεστι θεάσασθαι καὶ ζωγραφίας ἀλήθειαν παρὰ τὴν δημώδη καὶ μουσικῆς σεμνότητα παρὰ τὴν ἀκόλαστον. καὶ φιλοσοφίας οὖν ἐστιν ἀλήθειά τις παρὰ τοὺς ἄλλους φιλοσόφους καὶ κάλλος ἀληθινὸν παρὰ τὸ δεδολωμένον. οὔκουν ποτὲ τὰς ἐπὶ μέρους ἀληθείας, καθ’ ὧν ἡ ἀλήθεια κατηγορεῖται, αὐτὴν δὲ τὴν ἀλήθειαν πολυπραγμονητέον, οὐκ ὀνόματα ζητοῦντας μαθεῖν· τὸ γὰρ περὶ θεοῦ πρᾶγμα οὐκ ἔστιν ἕν, ἀλλὰ μυρία, διαφέρει δὲ τὸν θεὸν ζητεῖν ἢ τὰ περὶ θεοῦ. καθόλου δὲ εἰπεῖν περὶ ἑκάστου πράγματος τῆς οὐσίας τὰ συμβεβηκότα διακριτέον. Καί μοι ἀπόχρη φάναι θεὸν εἶναι τὸν κύριον πάντων. αὐτοτελῶς λῶς δὲ λέγω τὸν κύριον πάντων, οὐδενὸς ὑπολειπομένου κατὰ ἐξαίρεσιν. ἐπεὶ τοίνυν δύο εἰσὶν ἰδέαι τῆς ἀληθείας, τά τε ὀνόματα καὶ τὰ πράγματα, οἳ μὲν τὰ ὀνόματα λέγουσιν, οἱ περὶ τὰ κάλλη τῶν λόγων διατρίβοντες, οἱ παρ’ Ἕλλησι φιλόσοφοι, τὰ πράγματα δὲ παρ’ ἡμῖν ἐστι τοῖς βαρβάροις.
pass_a_gloss: But, as it seems, the philosophers of the Greeks, calling him God, do not know him, since they do not reverence God in a godly manner. The things philosophized by them, according to Empedocles, have come to us in vain through many tongues, seeing little of the whole. For just as the sun's light, through a vessel full of water, is contrived by art into fire, so also philosophy, taking the spark from divine scripture, is made manifest in a few things. For just as all living things breathe the same air, but in different ways and to different purposes, so also most people go through the truth, or rather the discourse about truth. They do not speak about God, but, carrying their own passions to God, they explain them. For they have made their life the pursuit of what is plausible, not what is true; and truth is not taught by imitation, but by learning. We do not believe in Christ so that we may seem to be good, just as we do not pass by the sun only to seem to be in the sun, but rather we strive to be good and virtuous for the sake of being Christians, because the kingdom is especially for those who strive, from seeking and learning and complete exercise, to become kings. The one imitating appearance deceives and takes away foresight. When someone, having taken a spark from the thing, ignites it within their soul with longing and learning, they set everything in motion towards knowledge. For what someone does not take hold of, they do not long for, nor do they embrace the benefit from it. The Gnostic, then, imitates the Lord at the end of their accomplishments, as far as is possible for humans, having taken on a certain lordly quality for the sake of likeness to God. Those who do not know knowledge cannot regulate the truth. It is not possible to partake of Gnostic theories unless we empty ourselves of prior thoughts. For truth is commonly said to be of all that is intelligible and sensible. Immediately, one can see the truth of painting, beyond the common, and the dignity of music, beyond the intemperate. And there is a truth of philosophy, beyond the other philosophers, and a true beauty, beyond the counterfeit. We should not, then, be concerned with partial truths, according to which truth is categorized, but with truth itself, not seeking to learn names, for the matter of God is not one, but many, and it differs to seek God or the things about God. In general, to speak about each thing's substance, the accidents must be distinguished. And it is enough for me to say that God is the Lord of all. I speak of the Lord of all in a self-sufficient way, leaving nothing out by exception. Since, then, there are two ideas of truth, names and things, those who speak about names, who spend their time on the beauties of words, the philosophers among the Greeks, and those who have things, are among us, the barbarians.

choices.why: to distinguish between complete and incomplete truths
to indicate a sudden or direct understanding
to refer to the concept of truth, rather than a specific truth

pass_b_english: As it appears, the Greek philosophers call him God but do not truly know him, because they do not reverence God as God deserves. Their philosophical systems, as Empedocles describes them, have come down to us through many tongues in vain, having seen only a tiny fraction of the whole. Just as a craftsman can focus the sun's light through a water-filled glass vessel to produce fire, so philosophy takes a spark from divine Scripture and makes it visible in only a few things. In the same way that all living creatures breathe the same air, yet each does so differently and for a different purpose, most people engage with the truth—or rather, with the discourse about truth. They do not speak about God; instead, they project their own passions onto God and then explain them. They have made their lives a pursuit of what is plausible rather than what is true, yet truth is not taught by imitation but by learning.

We do not believe in Christ merely to appear good, just as we do not step into the sunlight only to be seen in it. Rather, we strive to become good and virtuous for the sake of being Christians, because the kingdom belongs especially to those who strive—through seeking, learning, and complete discipline—to become kings. The one who imitates mere appearance deceives himself and loses true foresight. But when someone takes a spark from reality and kindles it within the soul with longing and learning, that person sets everything in motion toward genuine knowledge. For whoever does not grasp a thing will neither long for it nor welcome the benefit that comes from it. Consequently, the Gnostic, at the culmination of their achievements, imitates the Lord as far as humanly possible, receiving a lordly quality for the sake of likeness to God. Those who lack this knowledge cannot regulate the truth. It is impossible to share in Gnostic insights unless we first empty ourselves of prior conceptions.

Truth is properly said of everything that is intelligible and sensible. One can immediately perceive the truth of painting beyond the commonplace, and the dignity of music beyond the intemperate. Likewise there is a truth of philosophy beyond the other philosophers, and a true beauty beyond the counterfeit. We must not, then, busy ourselves with partial truths—those by which truth is categorized—but with truth itself, not seeking merely to learn names. For the matter of God is not a single thing but many, and seeking God differs from seeking the things about God. In general, when speaking of the substance of each thing, one must distinguish its accidents. It is enough for me to say that God is the Lord of all. I speak of the Lord of all in a self-sufficient way, leaving nothing out by exception. Since there are two kinds of truth—names and things—those who speak of names, who devote themselves to the beauties of words, are the philosophers among the Greeks; but those who possess the things themselves are among us, the barbarians.
